title: A Whole List of Reasons to Consider Marrying Young
author: Tim Challies
summary: Tim Challies argues, against both secular and church culture, that Christian young people should at least remain open to marrying young. He is careful to frame this as openness rather than prescription, insisting there is nothing wrong with marrying later. The article then assembles a cumulative list of reasons: the joy of building a life together from nothing, the biblical language of the wife of one’s youth, the counter-cultural witness of marriage over cohabitation, and the value of more years of mutual help. He also addresses practical and biological considerations, including that the Bible sets no wealth or career threshold for marriage, that decisions tend to get harder with age, and that fertility, family size and involvement with grandchildren all favour starting earlier. Challies resurfaced this piece, originally published in 2024, as a flashback item in his A La Carte roundup.
points: Challies frames his case as openness rather than a rule, repeatedly insisting that waiting to marry is not wrong.
He argues that marrying young and building a life together from nothing is a distinct joy, and that young marriage is a counter-cultural witness against serial relationships and cohabitation.
He questions the conventional thresholds of home ownership and career success, noting the Bible sets no such prerequisites for marriage.
His pastoral observation is that Christians who marry older are just as likely, perhaps more likely, to struggle in marriage.
Biology and time favour earlier marriage in fertility, family size and the length of involvement with grandchildren.
quotes: Over the past few decades, marriage in many Western countries has transformed from a rite-of-passage into adulthood to something more like an optional add-on to middle-age.

Contra the culture both within and outside of the church, I remain an advocate of marrying young. That’s not to say that there is anything wrong with waiting to marry until you are older or that you should marry young. However, I do suggest you at least be open to the possibility of it.

There is something sweet and significant about building a life together. While there is nothing wrong with building separate lives and then combining them in your late twenties or thirties, it is a special joy to begin with nothing and build it all as a couple.

I have only anecdotal evidence to offer here, but it has been my personal and pastoral observation that Christians who marry older are just as likely (and maybe even more likely) to experience difficulties in their marriage.

While many cultural conventions dictate the importance of establishing a certain level of wealth or achieving a certain level of vocational success before getting married, the Bible does not. You can get married without owning a home or beginning your first career.
Societal norms about the age of childbirth have changed substantially and so too have reproductive technologies. But human biology has not.
The younger you have children, the younger you will be when you have grandchildren and thus be able to have longer and deeper involvement in their lives.

Instead, as you reach your late teens and early twenties and head into adulthood, begin to think, “I am now old enough to marry.” Then begin to pray and consider whether it would be wise and good to marry sooner rather than later.
